title: Medication & IV Safety
html:
Safe medication care is a reasoning process: verify the order, client, medication, dose, route, timing, allergies, indication, relevant assessment, and monitoring plan. Technology supports these checks but does not replace judgment.

Stop at uncertainty

  • Hold and clarify an incomplete, illegible, contraindicated, or unexpectedly dosed order.
  • Use independent verification for high-alert medications when policy requires it.
  • Know what effect and adverse response you are monitoring before administration.
After administration
Document accurately and reassess the outcome. A medication is not safely given until the client's response is considered.

Watch the access site and the client

For parenteral therapy, assess line patency, site condition, compatibility, rate, and systemic response. If infiltration, extravasation, reaction, or overload is suspected, stop or pause the source as appropriate, assess, and follow the medication- and facility-specific protocol.

Reconcile transitions

Compare what the client was taking with new orders at admission, transfer, and discharge. Resolve duplications, omissions, interactions, and unclear instructions before they reach the client.

Learning goals

Identify when to withhold an unsafe dose, protect injection and IV access safety, and describe reassessment after administration. Detailed drug classes and calculations are covered later in Pharmacology.

At the bedside

Use two approved identifiers, compare the medication with the current order, and check allergies and the reaction history. Review the indication, recent doses, relevant laboratory results and assessment findings, route, formulation, and required monitoring. For example, a medication may be ordered but unsafe to give before an abnormal pre-administration assessment is clarified. Barcode scanning and smart pumps can detect some errors but cannot decide whether the medication is appropriate for this client now.

If a dose seems unusual, hold that dose while promptly clarifying with the prescriber and pharmacist. Do not independently substitute a familiar dose. A client's question or refusal is an opportunity to reassess and explain; document the actual administration or refusal, never a dose that has not been taken.

Prevent contamination and line errors

Use a new sterile needle and syringe for each injection and do not share single-dose containers between clients. Follow aseptic access procedures. Trace tubing from the client to its source before connecting or changing an infusion, and verify compatibility rather than mixing unfamiliar medications based on appearance.

Infiltration is not the same as extravasation

Swelling, coolness, discomfort, or leakage may mean fluid has left the vein. Stop the infusion and assess the drug and site. If a tissue-damaging drug may have extravasated, do not flush or immediately discard the access: retain the catheter initially for possible aspiration or agent-specific treatment, notify the appropriate team, and follow the drug-specific protocol. Catheter removal, antidotes, and warm or cold compresses depend on the agent and protocol. Do not improvise a universal treatment.

Close the loop

Record the dose, route, time, site when relevant, withheld doses and communication, and the client's response. Reassess at a time appropriate to the medication and route. Relief of symptoms does not remove the need to check for adverse effects.

Sources for review

  • CDC: Safe injection practices
  • NHS: Extravasation management

Original educational synthesis. Local protocols and qualified faculty guide clinical application.
